definition: Satirical means using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize or mock foolishness.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word satirical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know satirical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The late-night show's satirical sketch "thanked" smartphone makers for finally freeing families from the burden of dinner conversation.
Playful teasing amuses without any real target; satirical humor aims its jokes at a genuine flaw.
Scathing criticism burns without needing jokes at all—harsher than satirical wit.

Mocking covers any ridicule at all — a sneer, a cruel imitation, a scornful laugh — with no method required. Satirical ridicule works through humor and clever overstatement, and it aims at a real flaw worth exposing. All satire mocks; most mocking has none of satire's craft or purpose.

Tongue-in-cheek describes playful insincerity — saying what you don't quite mean, with a wink, purely for fun. Satirical work borrows that wink and points it at a target: the humor exists to criticize a real foolishness. A tongue-in-cheek toast teases; a satirical sketch indicts.

Sardonic names a tone — scornful, biting, darkly amused — that can color a single remark and needs no purpose beyond itself. Satirical names a project: using humor, irony, or exaggeration to expose a real flaw. A sardonic aside mocks the moment; satirical work is built around its target.
Earnest expression means every word sincerely, with no hidden mockery.
Reverent treatment honors its subject rather than poking fun at it.

The over-the-top praise is not sincere—it uses humor and absurd overstatement to poke fun at the cafeteria food.
Mockery delivered through comedy is what makes something satirical rather than plain criticism.
Reach for satirical when humor carries a critique: cartoons, sketch shows, mock news stories.
If a piece is funny but attacks nothing, it is merely comic; if it attacks without humor, it is plain criticism.
Satire needs both the joke and the target.

For its April issue, the student paper ran a glowing 'tribute' to Ridgeline High's new six-minute lunch.
The article thanked administrators for 'freeing students from the tyranny of chewing' and proposed medals for anyone who finished a sandwich before the bell.
It was satirical from the first line: the praise was absurd on purpose, and every exaggeration pointed at the same real problem — a lunch too short to eat.
A few parents read it straight and called to congratulate the principal, which the editors counted as proof the joke had teeth.
The next month, the schedule committee quietly added nine minutes, and the paper ran a sincere thank-you no one mistook for a joke.
